summary: Describes a common format for encapsulating Fibre Channel (FC) frames so they can be carried over IP networks, and a procedure for measuring and computing frame transit time through the IP network. It is meant for use by any IETF protocol that encapsulates FC frames.

eli5.summary: Fibre Channel frames are packages for storage-area networks. This puts them inside regular Internet envelopes so they can travel over ordinary networks, and measures how long the trip takes.

subtitle: A common wrapper that lets Fibre Channel frames travel over TCP/IP, with a timestamp to enforce frame lifetime.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel frames need to cross IP networks, but each encapsulating protocol would otherwise invent its own wrapper and its own way to keep frames from outliving the Fibre Channel lifetime limit.
tldr.mechanism: A 7-word header carries a protocol number, version, flags, frame length and a timestamp, with one's complement copies or a CRC to validate it. The frame itself follows, bracketed by SOF and EOF delimiter words.
tldr.outcome: FCIP and iFCP, the first two protocols assigned numbers, can share one format. Each encapsulating protocol still has to define its own security, synchronization and forwarding policies.

today: RFC 3643 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It still defines the common FC frame encapsulation that encapsulating protocols such as FCIP and iFCP refer to.

sections.title: Scope and Restrictions
sections.content:
RFC 3643 describes common mechanisms for carrying Fibre Channel (FC) frames over an IP network. It covers the encapsulation format and a way to enforce the lifetime limits that Fibre Channel places on frames. It is intended for use by any IETF protocol that encapsulates FC frames.

The standards body for Fibre Channel, INCITS Technical Committee T11, decided that some functions and modes are not interoperable to the degree the IETF needs (see FC-MI). The RFC folds those determinations in as restrictions on the encapsulation.

The RFC warns readers who know Fibre Channel that both Fibre Channel and IETF standards use the same byte transmission order, but the bit and byte numbering differs. Appendix A shows how to read the diagrams with Fibre Channel numbering.
sections.eli5: This document makes one standard box for sending Fibre Channel parcels through the Internet, so everyone packs them the same way.

sections.title: Encapsulation Concepts
sections.content:
The smallest unit of data transmission and routing in Fibre Channel is the frame. A frame consists of a Start Of Frame (SOF) delimiter, the FC frame content, and an End Of Frame (EOF) delimiter. FC frames are variable length and always include a CRC that detects errors in the contents.

To carry a frame over an IP-based transport such as TCP, the native frame is placed inside a slightly larger structure: an encapsulation header, then the SOF, the FC frame content, and the EOF. All of these are mapped to TCP in big endian byte order, the standard network byte order.

The FC frame content is the data between the SOF and EOF delimiters, including the FC CRC. Its 8-bit bytes can be sent directly. The SOF and EOF, however, are special 10-bit characters in Fibre Channel's 8b/10b link encoding that have no 8-bit equivalent, so they need their own byte codes (see the frame format section).
sections.eli5: A Fibre Channel frame is a parcel with a start flag and an end flag. To mail it over the Internet, we put it in a slightly bigger box with a shipping label on top.

sections.title: The FC Encapsulation Header
sections.content:
The header is seven 32-bit words. Word 0 holds Protocol#, Version and their one's complements -Protocol# and -Version, each one byte. Words 1 and 2 are Encapsulating Protocol Specific, whose meaning is defined by whichever protocol uses the encapsulation. Word 3 holds Flags, Frame Length and their complements. Words 4 and 5 are the timestamp, and word 6 is a CRC.

  • Protocol# says which encapsulating protocol is in use, with values assigned by IANA.
  • Version SHALL be 0x01. All other values are reserved.
  • Frame Length counts the whole encapsulated frame, header and SOF/EOF words included, in 32-bit words.
  • The only defined flag is CRCV. A value of one means the CRC field is valid. It SHALL be constant for all headers sent on a connection.
  • Reserved flag bits SHALL be zero on send. Receivers MAY check for zero, but that could break compatibility with future versions.
sections.eli5: The label on the box says who packed it, which version of the rules was used, how big the box is, and when it was sent. Each important number is written twice, once flipped, so mistakes are easy to spot.

sections.title: Validating the Header
sections.content:
Two mechanisms check that a candidate header is real. Redundancy-based validation relies on the duplicated, one's complemented fields. Receivers SHOULD either validate the CRC or compare each field with its complement. The check is stepwise, word by word, so a bad header can be rejected before all of it has arrived. Encapsulating protocols that use this approach SHOULD define how receivers use the complement fields.

CRC-based validation relies on the CRC in the last word. When CRCV is zero the CRC field SHALL be zero. When it is one, the field holds a CRC over words 0 to 5, computed with the polynomial, initial value and bit order defined for Fibre Channel in FC-FS, and sent in FC-2 format. The receiver recomputes it over all bytes before the CRC word and compares.

The two mechanisms suit two different design and operating environments.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to check the label was not smudged: compare each number with its flipped twin, or run a quick math check over the whole label.

sections.title: Measuring Frame Transit Time
sections.content:
An FC Fabric must limit the lifetime of a frame. When part of the path is an IP connection, the time spent crossing it counts toward that limit. So the sender records the departure time in the header, and if both ends have synchronized clocks the receiver can compute the transit time. The two timestamp words use the time format of SNTP version 4: seconds since 0 hour on 1 January 1900, plus a fraction of a second. Zero in both words means no valid timestamp.

An entity that does not support transit time calculation SHALL send zeros and ignore received timestamps. One that does must have a stable internal time base and one synchronized with the other entities it talks to. The encapsulating protocol must describe how to synchronize.

Each entity is either Synchronized or Unsynchronized. It starts Unsynchronized at power-up, becomes Synchronized once its time base is aligned, and MUST drop back if it cannot keep sync. In the Synchronized state a sender records its time base in the header. A receiver with a valid timestamp computes transit time as its own time minus the recorded departure time, and handles the result and the frame as the encapsulating protocol says. If both words are zero it de-encapsulates without computing transit time.

In the Unsynchronized state, whether frames are processed at all is up to the encapsulating protocol. If they are, the entity sends zero timestamps and ignores received ones.
sections.eli5: Parcels must not be too old when they arrive, so each one is stamped with the time it left. If the sender's and receiver's clocks agree, the receiver can work out how long the trip took.

sections.title: SOF and EOF Words
sections.content:
An encapsulated frame is the header, then an SOF word, the FC frame content, and an EOF word. The FC frame content is always a multiple of four bytes. Each delimiter word repeats its code twice, followed by two copies of the one's complement (-SOF and -EOF), so that transmission errors are protected against. Receivers SHOULD validate these fields according to a policy defined by the encapsulating protocol.

Table 2 gives the SOF codes: SOFf is 0x28, SOFi2 0x2D, SOFn2 0x35, SOFi3 0x2E, SOFn3 0x36, SOFi4 0x29, SOFn4 0x31 and SOFc4 0x39. Table 3 gives the EOF codes: EOFn 0x41, EOFt 0x42, EOFni 0x49, EOFa 0x50, EOFdt 0x46, EOFdti 0x4E, EOFrt 0x44 and EOFrti 0x4F.

FC-BB-2 lists further SOF and EOF codes, such as SOFi1 and SOFn1. FC-MI identifies them as not interoperable, so this RFC leaves them out.
sections.eli5: The start and end flags are special symbols that cannot be sent as ordinary bytes, so each gets a code number, written twice with flipped copies to catch mistakes.

sections.title: What Encapsulating Protocols Must Define
sections.content:
The encapsulation leaves much to the protocols that use it. Appendix B collects the obligations. An encapsulating protocol SHALL specify its IANA-assigned Protocol#, the contents of the Encapsulating Protocol Specific field, and how receivers verify that a header is being processed correctly.

It SHALL also define how over-age frames are detected: whether transit time measurement is optional, the stability and resolution required of the time base, how clocks are synchronized and when an entity is Synchronized, whether frames flow while Unsynchronized, how to treat frames without a valid timestamp, and the transit time limit with what to do when a frame exceeds it.
sections.eli5: This standard box is only half the job. Each shipping company using it still has to write its own rules for clocks, late parcels and checking labels.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says only that this document describes the encapsulation format. Security depends on how an encapsulating protocol uses it, so each such protocol SHALL describe its own security considerations in its own document.

For IANA, the Protocol# field values come from a new registry. Value 0 should not be assigned until all others have been. Values 240 to 255 are set aside for private use among cooperating systems. Other values go only to Standards Track RFCs approved by the IESG. This RFC allocates value 1 to FCIP (Fibre Channel over TCP/IP) and value 2 to iFCP.
sections.eli5: The box does not lock anything by itself. Whoever uses the box must say how to keep it safe, and a number registry keeps each user's label number from clashing.

fields.name: Protocol#
fields.desc: Which encapsulating protocol is in use; assigned by IANA.

fields.name: Encapsulating Protocol Specific (word 1)
fields.desc: Meaning defined by the encapsulating protocol.

fields.name: Encapsulating Protocol Specific (word 2)
fields.desc: Meaning defined by the encapsulating protocol.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved bits plus the CRCV flag.

fields.name: CRC
fields.desc: CRC over words 0 to 5 when CRCV is one; otherwise zero.
